[MUQATIL:12:16-18/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Joseph’s brothers come to Jacob at the evening prayer, claiming they went hunting and left Joseph guarding their belongings; the wolf ate him, they say, and Jacob will not believe them even if truthful.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايلحقالتاءوالكافاللتينللإضمارإذاجاوزتالواحد)#744/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For dual and masculine plural suffixes, add mīm after the dual alif or plural wāw; no further marker is added beyond two because dual is already a plural form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايلحقالتاءوالكافاللتينللإضمارإذاجاوزتالواحد)#744/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The dual or plural suffixes -tumā and -tumū keep ḍamma on tāʾ and kāf; number and gender are marked by what follows, so the singleton vowels are no longer used.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايلحقالتاءوالكافاللتينللإضمارإذاجاوزتالواحد)#744/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Feminine plural verb endings do not double nūn, unlike pronoun suffixes such as -tun and -kunna; doubling is avoided to prevent four or five consecutive vowels in one word.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكأنهلايجوزأنيقولالرجلرأيتعبداللهفتقولمنالأنهإذاذكر#452/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After someone names a definite person such as ʿAbd Allāh, asking منه is inappropriate because the speaker means someone identified individually; one may ask who he is or which man.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكأنهلايجوزأنيقولالرجلرأيتعبداللهفتقولمنالأنهإذاذكر#452/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · العرب | reports | Some Arabs nevertheless ask مع منين after ذهبنا معهم or منا after رأيته when the referents are not personally known; they treat the report like رأيت رجلا.

[QURTUBI-FULL:12:17#3/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Horse and camel races require a known finish and distance; archery also requires a known target, number of rounds, and agreed hit criterion such as piercing through or another specified strike.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:17#3/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The first permitted prize arrangement is a ruler or other donor voluntarily offering a known award to the winner; the second is a one-sided stake, which the winner may take and the loser does not reclaim, with no scholarly disagreement.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:17#3/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | When both racers stake money for the winner, the arrangement is only permitted with a third entrant who could beat either: if the entrant wins, he takes both stakes; if either racer wins, that racer takes both, and the entrant neither pays nor receives.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:17#3/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو علي بن خيران | reports | Abu ʿAli ibn Khayran says the third, qualifying horse's racing ability must be unknown; he is called a muhallil because his participation makes the wager lawful.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:17#3/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Scholars agree that when both racers stipulate that the winner takes the other's stake and there is no qualifying third entrant, the arrangement is gambling and forbidden.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:17#4/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | A Prophetic report says a horse inserted between two is not gambling if its ability to beat them is uncertain, but is gambling if it is certain to lose; Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib similarly permits a horse wager with a qualifying entrant, as do al-Shafiʿi and most scholars.
[QURTUBI-FULL:12:17#4/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Al-Mubarrad and Ibn Ishaq take “wa-law kunna” to mean “even if we were” or “even though we were.”
